title: Infant gut anellovirus composition associates with early life factors and childhood atopic disease

paper_content.abstract: Anelloviruses are single-stranded circular DNA viruses that infect eukaryotic cells. They are acquired in infancy and can be found in most body compartments. The Anelloviridae family is highly prevalent and genetically diverse, but factors shaping the composition and the relationship with disease remain elusive. Here, we characterise faecal viromes of 647 one-year-old children from the deeply phenotyped Copenhagen Prospective Studies on Asthma in Childhood (COPSAC 2010) mother-child cohort. In this study, 111 unique anellovirus species are identified and reveal immense prevalence and individual variability. The anellovirus and bacteriophage compositions are slightly correlated, while no correlation is observed with the bacterial composition. Early-life exposures such as attending daycare and having older siblings are associated with a reduced anellovirus abundance and diversity, and influence the anellovirus composition. Additionally, genetic secretors of the FUT2 enzyme have a higher anellovirus abundance compared to non-secretors. Minor associations are observed between anelloviruses and later allergic rhinitis, but no associations are found for concurrent acute infections or the development of other atopic traits. Our findings indicate that anelloviruses are a commensal component of all infants’ faecal virome, and further investigations into how immune-training factors influence their composition longitudinally are pertinent.
paper_content.introduction:
The gut microbiome is composed of millions of microorganisms, including bacteria and viruses. It is established in infancy and is influenced by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors, such as delivery mode, nutrition, host genetics and environmental exposures. An increasing body of research is finding links between the gut microbiome and acute and chronic diseases. Current research is largely focused on the bacterial component of the gut microbiome and, to some extent bacteriophages. However, the members of the highly prevalent Anelloviridae family infect human cells and showcase a considerably high abundance in some individuals. Despite this, it is still largely unknown how these viruses colonise the host, which factors influence this colonisation, and how they may influence health and disease in childhood.

Anelloviruses are single-stranded circular DNA viruses that infect eukaryotic cells and exhibit an immense genetic diversity. They are highly prevalent, believed to be present in nearly all humans across the earth, and have been found in a multitude of sample types ranging from skin, saliva and blood, to faeces. Coinfections with anelloviruses of multiple different genotypes in one individual also commonly appear, especially in early life.

Anelloviruses are acquired in infancy, potentially already through transplacental transmission, considering that anelloviruses have been identified in umbilical cord blood, amniotic fluid and newborns, though the findings are not entirely concordant. Mothers and their infants shared some, but not all, anelloviruses in the blood. Similarly, adult twins share less faecal anelloviruses than child twins. Several potential sources of transmission have been suggested, such as breast milk or contact with skin, hair or saliva from infected individuals, though there is conflicting evidence. Moreover, birth mode may influence the anellovirus composition, as one study found that children born by spontaneous vaginal delivery exhibited larger gut anelloviral diversity than children born by emergency Caesarean section. Anelloviral richness in blood and faeces has been shown to be low during the first few weeks and months of life, possibly because unknown factors in mother’s milk protect against infection. Subsequently, with weaning, both richness and abundance increase between 6 to 15 months of age. Thereafter, it appears that the faecal anelloviral load decreases, demonstrated by a lower faecal anelloviral richness in mothers compared to infants, which could reflect infant immunity development that is partly dependent on maternal antibodies and the host’s own immune maturation.

Due to their high prevalence, anelloviruses are not believed to be causal in acute or chronic disease development, but this remains an intense topic of investigation. Furthermore, it has been speculated that direct interactions with the developing immune system in childhood could potentially affect the risk of developing immune disorders such as asthma and allergy. On one hand, anelloviruses from several sample types have reportedly been associated with a range of diseases such as IBD (faeces), fever (plasma), cancer (cancer tissue) and asthma (airways, plasma). On the other hand, another study reported no association of intestinal anelloviruses with type 1 diabetes development or seroconversion. In summary, there is a lack of concrete evidence that anelloviruses are causal in disease, and it remains unknown whether certain anelloviral species have more pathogenic potential than others.

In this study, we characterise the infant gut anellovirus composition in 647 children from the deeply phenotyped Copenhagen Prospective Studies on Asthma in Childhood (COPSAC 2010) cohort at age 1 year. The faecal viromes were previously sequenced and meticulously catalogued and described, identifying hundreds of novel viral families. The concurrent bacterial and bacteriophage compositions have previously been associated with asthma development. With this study, we aim to describe the composition and intrinsic and extrinsic shaping factors of the anelloviruses in early life and its association with infection susceptibility and development of the atopic diseases asthma, eczema and allergy.
paper_content.results:
Characterisation of the early-life virome
We analysed the sequencing data from DNA viruses extracted from faecal samples of 647 1-year-old children in the COPSAC 2010 cohort (Table 1). The early-life faecal virome consisted mainly of bacteriophages, but also contained two families of eukaryotic DNA viruses, namely the adenoviruses and anelloviruses. We have previously presented a deep characterisation of the bacteriophageome and its relation to asthma, as well as a report on the associations of environmental exposures on the overall gut virome in the same cohort. Even though the bacteriophages accounted for the vast majority of relative abundance in most samples (median = 97%, range = 7−100%), the anelloviruses were the most abundant eukaryotic viral family (median = 2%, range = 0−93%), while adenoviruses dominated in just a few individuals (median = 0%, range = 0−76%) (Fig. 1A). More than 9000 unique species of bacteriophages were identified, whereas the anelloviruses consisted of 111 unique species (970 viral OTUs or vOTUs) and the adenoviruses only comprised five unique species (Fig. 1B).

Infant gut anelloviruses are taxonomically diverse
vOTUs were delineated by virome assembly and deduplication at 95% nucleotide identity, where after anelloviral vOTUs were defined based on encoded protein similarity. After aligning the resulting 970 anelloviral vOTUs against anellovirus type species from the ICTV (International Committee for Taxonomy of Viruses website) and constructing an average nucleotide identity (ANI)-based tree (Fig. 2), we found that most (711, 73%) of the vOTUs belonged to the genus betatorquevirus, while alpha- and gammatorquevirus comprised a smaller fraction of the vOTUs. Furthermore, we found that 22 vOTUs formed two genus-level clades of their own that were related to, but separate from alpha- and gammatorquevirus respectively. Here, we propose naming these novel anelloviral genera phitorquevirus and tautorquevirus. They were present in 39% and 49% of the children, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 1A). The 970 anelloviral vOTUs were further grouped into species, using the recent ICTV-ratified anellovirus species cutoff at >35% average nucleotide divergence (100-ANI = AND). This yielded 111 distinct species. In order to bridge the large gap between the more than 100 species and the few genera, we defined anellovirus subgenera by cutting the tree at a depth corresponding to 50%, resulting in 36 anelloviral subgenera, which were named according to the genus to which they belonged. In further analyses, we calculated alpha and beta diversity at the species level; however, focused taxa-specific analyses at the subgenus and genus level for improved interpretability and to reduce the multiple testing burden.

Anelloviruses do not associate with common childhood infections
We tested the associations of acute infections (gastroenteritis, cold, and fever) on the total relative abundance of the bacteriophages, adenoviruses and anelloviruses in the COPSAC 2010 cohort. Participants with reported gastroenteritis symptoms within 7 days of faecal sampling had a significantly higher total adenovirus relative abundance (log2 fold change = 2.4, p < 0.047, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Fig. 1C). The total relative abundance of anelloviruses and bacteriophages were not related to any acute symptoms (p > 0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Fig. 1C). Since the role of adenoviruses on infections is already well established we excluded them from further analysis, and focused on the unexplored anelloviruses.

Anelloviruses are uniquely yet highly prevalent in the 1-year-old infant gut
As we demonstrated previously for bacteriophages, the anelloviruses were highly unique for each individual at the vOTU level, with 80% of the anellovirus vOTUs characterised as rare (present in 1−20% of participants), and only four vOTUs (0.4%) were part of the core anelloviruses (present in >50% of participants) (Fig. 1D). However, at the species, subgenus and genus level, the anelloviruses were increasingly shared among participants, and all samples contained at least one anellovirus. The anellovirus subgenera ranged in prevalence from 4% of participants (subgenus gamma 3 virus), to the subgenus betatorquevirus 1 (beta 1) being present in 100% of participants (Fig. 3A). The prevalence, median relative abundance and species richness of the anelloviral subgenera and genera were strongly associated (Fig. 3A and Supplementary Fig. 1A). However there were exceptions, such as the subgenus tautorquevirus 1 (tau 1) with a median relative abundance of 0, a prevalence of 49% and consisting of only 1 observed species (Fig. 3A). Interestingly, there did not appear to be a competitive (inverse) relationship among most anelloviruses, and there were some subgenera that were highly positively correlated (Fig. 3B and Supplementary Data 1). The alpha, beta, and gamma genera were all present in 100% of the samples, while the two previously undescribed genera we identified in this study, tautorquevirus and phitorquevirus, were present in 49 and 39% of the children, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 1A). Similar to the subgenera, the anelloviral genera showed largely positive correlations, in particular, the beta and alpha genera were highly correlated with each other, but also gamma and beta were significantly correlated (Supplementary Fig. 1B and Supplementary Data 1). Of the 111 anellovirus species detected in the cohort, each child carried on average 43 unique species (range = 9−86). The most prevalent anellovirus species was the alphatorquevirus 3, which was present in 631 (98%) of the children, whereas the least common species was the phitorquevirus 57, which was only present in 11 (2%) of the children in our cohort. Furthermore, we found that the anellovirus composition was significantly associated with the bacteriophageome (Procrustes, Supplementary Fig. 2A), but it was not associated with the bacterial composition as determined by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing (Supplementary Fig. 2B).

Extrinsic and intrinsic factors associated with the anellovirus alpha diversity and abundance
How anelloviruses colonise the host in early life and what factors influence the anellovirus composition is still not fully known. To shed light on this, we analysed the total anellovirus relative abundance and Faith’s phylogenetic diversity (PD) in relation to several social, environmental, genetic, pre-, peri- and postnatal factors. Using a generalised linear model adjusted for technical covariates, we found several significant links (Fig. 4A and Supplementary Data 2). The pregnant mothers in the COPSAC 2010 cohort took part in a randomised placebo-controlled fish oil intervention, which has been described previously. In the current study, we found that children born to mothers who received the fish oil intervention during pregnancy had a higher total relative anelloviral abundance (model estimate = 1.18 [1.03, 1.35], p = 0.05) and an increased Faith’s PD at 1 year of age (1.16 [1.00, 1.35], p = 0.02). There were no significant associations between high-dose Vitamin D intervention, delivery mode, or breastfeeding duration and anellovirus diversity or abundance. However, samples collected in the summer had a lower total anellovirus abundance and Faith’s PD compared to samples collected in other seasons (abundance: model estimate = 0.78, CI = [0.64, 0.96], p = 0.02, Faith’s PD: 0.80 [0.67, 0.97], p = 0.02). Similarly, children who had started daycare before faecal sampling had a lower anellovirus abundance and alpha diversity (abundance: 0.75 [0.62, 0.90], p = 0.002, Faith’s PD: 0.61 [0.52, 0.72], p = 1e-08), and the number of older siblings associated with a lower anellovirus abundance (abundance: 0.92 [0.86, 1.00], p = 0.04).

The FUT2 gene encodes the fucosyltransferase 2 enzyme, which determines a person’s histo-blood group antigen secretor status. Noroviruses and rotaviruses have been shown to bind to secreted histo-blood group antigens in the gut mucosa, and non-secretors demonstrate a decreased susceptibility to infection, thus we hypothesised that there may be a similar relationship for anelloviruses. Analysis of secretor status revealed that children who were secretors (GA or GG allele, N = 475) based on the SNP rs601338 had a significantly higher total relative anelloviral abundance compared to non-secretors (AA allele, N = 101) (1.28 per SD increase in abundance, [1.04, 1.59], p = 0.02), though there was no effect on Faith’s PD.

Extrinsic and intrinsic factors associated with the anellovirus beta diversity
When comparing all the previously mentioned extrinsic and intrinsic parameters against the overall anellovirus composition using several beta diversity metrics, we again identified significant associations (Fig. 4B and Supplementary Data 3). Some perinatal factors, such as the mother’s antibiotic use at birth (Aitchison distance R2 = 0.2, p = 0.02) and whether the vaginal birth was induced (Aitchison distance R2 = 0.3, p = 0.002, Jaccard distance R2 = 0.4, p = 0.006) were significantly associated with the overall anellovirus composition. Concordant with the results on alpha diversity and overall relative anelloviral abundance, postnatal factors that may be involved in immune system development, such as whether children had started daycare before the faecal sampling, is associated with a significantly different anellovirus composition compared to children who had not yet started daycare (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and Jaccard and Aitchison distance R2 = 0.3, 0.5 and 0.2, respectively, all p < 0.05).

Extrinsic and intrinsic factors associated with the anellovirus taxa abundances
Finally, we associated the relative abundance of anelloviral subgenera and genera with all previously mentioned extrinsic and intrinsic parameters to investigate taxa-specific associations. Here we again found several strong signals in the same direction as for the analyses on overall anelloviral abundance (Fig. 4A). Particularly, being in daycare and the number of older siblings were negatively associated with anellovirus abundance across many subgenera, as were several birth-related factors such as sample date, season and induction (Fig. 5 and Supplementary Data 4, 5).

The anellovirus composition is linked to the gut bacterial maturation
Due to the numerous findings relating to the decreased anellovirus abundance and diversity with daycare start, we employed additional analyses to elucidate this relationship. We found that children who had entered daycare had a higher incidence of cold and fever (Chi-squared test, OR 1.63 [1.09−2.47], p = 0.02 and 2.02 [1.27−3.31], p = 0.003), though not gastroenteritis (1.25 [0.67−2.53], p = 0.48). Thus, we considered whether the lower abundance of anellovirus in children in daycare was a compositional decrease driven by an increased abundance of other eukaryotic viruses, such as adenovirus. However, we did not find an association between daycare attendance and the overall adenovirus abundance. We have previously calculated microbiota-by-age z-scores that capture the maturation of the bacterial component of the gut microbiome of the children in the COPSAC 2010 cohort. There was a slight negative correlation between the gut microbial maturation score and the overall relative anelloviral abundance (Spearman’s correlation rho = −0.08, p = 0.04).

The gut anellovirus composition does not associate with the development of childhood atopic disease
While the anellovirus composition was not associated with infections in the COPSAC 2010 cohort, previous studies have suggested potential links to chronic diseases and immune system development. Thus, we investigated the relationship between the anelloviruses and the development of asthma, allergic rhinitis or atopic dermatitis by age 6 years. The total relative anellovirus abundance and individual anellovirus diversity (alpha diversity, as measured by multiple metrics) was not associated with atopic dermatitis or asthma development (Figs. 6A, B, 7A, B and Supplementary Data 6). However, the anellovirus Shannon index and evenness were lower in children who developed allergic rhinitis by 6 years of age (Shannon index: estimate 0.6 [0.41, 0.98], p = 0.04 and evenness: 0.1 [0.01, 0.67], p = 0.01, Fig. 8A, B and Supplementary Data 6). We delved further into allergic sensitisation to food and inhaled allergens at ages 6 months, 18 months or 6 years. Here we found suggestive results of aeroallergen sensitisation at 18 months associated with evenness (estimate 0.04 [0.00, 1.20], p = 0.067) and Shannon index (0.54 [0.25, 1.09], p = 0.089), and food sensitisation at 6 years associated with inverse Simpson index (1.04 [1.00, 1.08], p = 0.058) (Supplementary Data 6). All other tests on allergic sensitisations were not significant. Likewise, the overall anellovirus composition (beta diversity, as measured by multiple dissimilarity metrics) was not associated with atopic dermatitis or asthma development (PERMANOVA adjusted for technical covariates, Figs. 6C, 7C and Supplementary Fig. 3A, B, 3C, D and Supplementary Data 7). Nevertheless, Bray-Curtis dissimilarity was significantly associated with allergic rhinitis development (F = 1.62, R2(%) = 0.26, p = 0.01, PERMANOVA adjusted for covariates, Fig. 8C and Supplementary Fig. 3E, F, and Supplementary Data 7). When investigating the beta diversity in relation to allergic sensitisation, we found several metrics to be significantly different between cases and controls of any sensitisation at 6 years and aeroallergen sensitisation at 6 years and a suggestive association with aeroallergen sensitisation at 6 months (Supplementary Data 7). All other tests on sensitisation were not significant.

To investigate the relationship between the gut anellovirus composition and atopic disease at a more detailed level, we tested the differential relative abundance of anelloviral genera, subgenera, and species for all three atopic diseases. None were significantly different (Supplementary Figs. 4A, D, G, 5A, D, G for subgenera and genera, respectively, Supplementary Data 8). In addition to this, we employed an indicator species analysis, aiming to find genera, subgenera, and species that were indicative of cases or controls for all three atopic diseases. None of the results were significant after adjusting for multiple testing (Supplementary Figs. 4B, C, E, F, H, I, 5B, C, E, F, H, I for subgenera and genera, respectively, Supplementary Data 9). Moreover, we employed two separate multivariate methods, namely sparse partial least squares regression (sPLS) and random forest, for investigating the relationship between the faecal anellovirus relative abundance at the species or subgenus level at age 1 year and the development of these atopic diseases. These methods did not yield sufficiently discriminatory results, with a median area under the curve (AUC) for the test set below 0.562 (Supplementary Data 10).
paper_content.methods:
Study population
The study is composed of samples collected in the Danish population-based Copenhagen Prospective Studies on Asthma in Childhood (COPSAC 2010) mother-child cohort. Samples were collected from 700 children and their mothers, starting at 24 weeks of pregnancy up to 6 years of age.

Inclusion and ethics
The study was conducted in accordance with the guiding principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the National Committee on Health Research Ethics (H-B-2008-093) and the Danish Data Protection Agency (2015-41-3696). Both parents gave written informed consent before enrolment.

Faecal sample collection, virome extraction and computational processing
Faecal samples from 660 children at 1 year of age were collected either by the parents following comprehensive instructions, or at the clinic. Samples were sent to the laboratory by post and mixed with 1 ml glycerol broth (10% vol/vol glycerol) on arrival and stored at −80°C. Detailed protocols on extraction and sequencing have been described previously. In short, to obtain viromes the faecal samples were filtered to enrich for viral particles and the DNA was extracted using the QIAmp viral RNA mini kit and underwent multiple displacement amplification for 30 min. The virome libraries were prepared following the manufacturer’s directions for the Illumina Nextera XT kit (FC-131-1096) and sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq X platform (2 × 150 bp paired-end reads), resulting in an average depth of 3 Gb per sample. The sequencing was successful for 647 of the 660 samples. The reads were filtered, trimmed using Fastq Quality Trimmer/Filter v0.0.14 (options -Q33 -t 13 -l 32 -p 90 -q 13), and adaptors were removed using cutadapt (v2.0). The processed reads were then de-replicated using VSEARCH (v2.4.3) “derep_prefix” and assembled with Spades (v3.10.1) using the meta flag with hamming disabled. Resulting contigs were deduplicated across all samples at the 95% average nucleotide identity (ANI)-level to yield vOTUs. Virus family-level clusters of vOTUs were first defined based on encoded protein similarity in order to identify all vOTUs belonging to the anellovirus family. This protein-level identification step was to ensure sensitivity towards novel anelloviruses distant from those already found in public databases. The workflow is described in detail on GitHub (https://github.com/shiraz-shah/VFCs). In short, pairwise alignments (from FASTA v. 36) between all vOTU-encoded open reading frames were used to (1) construct an all-against-all vOTU distance matrix for a neighbour-joining tree that was cut deeply, at the virus family-level, and (2) for Markov Clustering in order to define viral gene families, that had their functions resolved by profile-profile alignment against the Pfam database. Finally, the family-level vOTU cluster that carried the anelloviral ORF1 gene family was selected as the anellovirus family in our data. Next, whole-genome Smith−Waterman alignments were made at the DNA-level, between all identified anelloviral vOTUs in addition to public genome representatives for all ICTV-ratified genera, all the way from alpha- to zayintorquevirus. The whole-genome nucleotide alignments were used to define pairwise distances for a neighbour-joining tree. The tree was rooted using iotatorquevirus (known to infect non-human mammals such as pigs) as an outgroup. Subsequently, cut distances from the root were measured that would reproduce all the ICTV genera. This revealed two additional and undescribed genera that were named based on the vacant Greek letters tau and phi. A similar species-level root cut distance was derived based on the reproduction of select ICTV species belonging to alpha, beta and gammatorquevirus. The representative ICTV species were chosen because they had been revised recently, thus likely comprising borderline cases with a rigorous and up-to-date application of the most recent ICTV species-level cutoff. Cutting the tree at a distance reproducing those species enabled comprehensive species-level resolution for the entire dataset. While inspecting the tree distances, an additional local minimum was found between the genus and species-level root distance, and this was used as the cut distance for defining anellovirus subgenera.

Bacterial extraction and computational processing
Details on the processing of faecal samples for 16S rRNA sequencing and processing have been published previously. In short, the bacterial DNA was extracted from the faecal samples using MoBio PowerSoil kits targeting the V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene and sequenced using the v2 kit on the Illumina MiSeq platform to generate paired-end 250 bp reads. Samples with more than 2000 reads were kept before primers were removed, the reads were trimmed and ASVs were inferred.

Clinical phenotypes
Asthma. The asthma diagnosis was assessed prospectively based on a quantitative symptom algorithm published previously. A case in this study defined as having ever had an asthma diagnosis by the age of 6 years.

Atopic dermatitis. The atopic dermatitis diagnosis was based on the criteria of Hanifin and Rajka and with clinical assessment throughout childhood. To be labelled as a case, at least three of four major criteria and at least 3 of 23 minor criteria were needed, and a case was considered as having ever had an atopic dermatitis diagnosis by the age of 6 years.

Allergic rhinitis. Allergic rhinitis at age 6 years was diagnosed based on allergic sensitisation and clinical interviews of the parents on history of significant nasal congestion, sneezing and/or runny nose outside periods with common cold and in the relevant period of exposure to the sensitised aeroallergen. If the participant did not self-report rhinitis, the participant was labelled as a control. If the participant self-reported rhinitis and at least one of the allergens was positive, the participant was labelled as a case. If the participant self-reported rhinitis and all allergens were negative, the participant was labelled as a control. If the participant self-reported rhinitis and the above-mentioned criteria for being a case was not fulfilled, and at least one of the allergens or antibodies were blank, the participant case status was set as missing. If the participant self-reported rhinitis but the IgE and skin prick test were inconclusive, the participant's case status was set as missing.

Infections. Symptoms of infections included colds, fever, and gastroenteritis within (+-) 7 days of the faecal sample were collected by daily diaries.

Covariates. Information on physician-diagnosed asthma in the mother and father, maternal age at birth, smoking during pregnancy, antibiotics in pregnancy, preeclampsia, gestational age, birth weight, C-section or vaginal birth, induction of birth, parents atopy, antibiotics administered to the child, pet ownership, older children in the home, introduction of foods (cow’s milk, eggs, fish and hypoallergenic formula), daycare start and duration of exclusive and total breastfeeding period was obtained during the scheduled visits to the research clinic. C-section was either encoded as 'C-section': any C-section (acute or planned) compared to any vaginal delivery (induced or spontaneous, or as 'Emergency C-section': acute C-section compared to spontaneous vaginal delivery. Information on intrapartum antibiotics was validated against birth records from hospitals, and information on antibiotic use during pregnancy and childhood was validated against national registries. The living environment was based on home address at birth using the CORINE satellite-based land cover database. Fish oil and high-dose vitamin D intervention groups in pregnancy were included.

Statistical analyses
All analyses were conducted in the programming language R version 4.2.2 (Vienna).

Preparation and normalisation of relative abundance data. We calculated the relative abundance per sample, including all viruses detected in our samples, because we wanted to investigate the role of anelloviruses relative to the entire virome community, partly due to the potential biological relationship between these viral compartments, as demonstrated by the procrustes analysis described in the results section 'Anelloviruses are uniquely yet highly prevalent in the 1-year-old infant gut'.

Technical covariates. Several analyses were adjusted for covariates as noted; the selected covariates were the proportion of viral reads, age at faecal sampling, sequencing lane and sequencing depth. These were chosen based on their relationship with the anellovirus composition as measured by several alpha and beta diversity measures.

Alpha and beta diversity calculations. Alpha diversity was calculated at the species level without filtering, with Faith’s phylogenetic diversity (PD) (package picante version 1.8.2), Shannon index, inverse Simpson’s index (phyloseq package version 1.44.0, estimate_richness function) and evenness (Shannon index divided by the number of observed species). Beta diversity was calculated at the vOTU level without filtering using Aitchison (pseudocount of half of the lowest non-zero value in the data), Bray-Curtis, Jaccard, Canberra (function vegdist from vegan package version 2.6-4) and Spearman distance (function separman.dist from bioDist package version 1.70.0), as well as weighted UniFrac and unweighted UniFrac distance (unifrac function from phyloseq package version 1.44.0). The difference in beta diversity between cases and controls was tested using a permutational multivariate analysis of variance using distance matrices (PERMANOVA, adonis2 function from the vegan package version 2.6-4), with 9999 permutations, sequencing lane set as strata, and covariates as described above.

Indicator species analysis. The relative abundance data was filtered to remove species with a prevalence < 50%, all subgenera and genera were included for analyses. Indicator species were identified with the multipatt function (999 permutations) from the indicspecies package version 1.7.14). This allows for the identification of particular taxa that are indicators of certain sample groups, such as cases or controls of clinical outcomes. Indicator species are defined as either being specific (positive predictive value, the probability that the sample belongs to a group due to the species being present) or being sensitive (the probability of finding the species in samples belonging to a group). Species displaying high specificity to a group occur only in samples from that group (though not necessarily present in all samples) and are missing from the samples of the other group. Species displaying high sensitivity to a group occur in all samples belonging to that group and are largely missing from samples of the other group.

Differential abundance analysis. Differential abundance of anellovirus taxa was tested with a generalised linear model (glm, family = 'binomial’) adjusted for the above-mentioned covariates, with the relative abundance zero mean unit variance scaled.

Secretor status analysis. Based on the genome-wide genotyping of the blood cell fraction of plasma using the Illumina OmniExpress imputed with the Hapmap and 1000 genomes reference populations, the rs601338 SNP was encoded to either non-secretors (AA allele, N = 101) or secretors (GA or GG allele, N = 475). The statistical test was performed using a generalised linear model (glm, family = 'binomial’) adjusted for the above-mentioned covariates.

Multivariate analyses using sPLS. Sparse partial least squares (sPLS) from the mixOmics package was used to test the multivariate association between the anelloviruses and clinical outcomes. This methodology maximises the covariance between latent variables of the data, rather than the variance explained on the outcome side. This results in a robust model that is resistant to overfitting and can handle high-dimensional data as both dependent and independent variables, even with small sample sizes. This model identifies linear combinations of the variables from the datasets as a measure to reduce the dimensionality of the data. The microbial data agglomerated at the species level was filtered to remove species with a prevalence < 30%, while at the subgenus level, all taxa were kept, before log transforming with a pseudocount of half of the minimum non-zero value. The data was then split into a training (80%) and testing (20%) set ten times (termed stability runs) using the function createDataPartition from the caret package version 6.0-94 to achieve stable estimates of the model accuracy, thus avoiding spurious results from certain sample combinations. The model was trained on the training set using the train function from the caret package with scale and centre as pre-processing, using fivefold repeated cross-validation with three repeats using the trainControl function. The hyperparameters used were keepX (number of taxa to keep) which started at 5 to the maximum number of taxa, with a step size of 4 for subgenera, and a step size of 8 for species, and ncomp (number of components) which was set to 1:4. The model hyperparameter set with the best median area under the curve (AUC) calculated across all repeats was selected and evaluated on the testing set. The median test AUC of the ten stability runs was used to evaluate the model performance.

Multivariate analyses using random forest. A random forest model was additionally used to test the multivariate association between the anelloviruses and clinical outcomes. This type of methodology can identify nonlinear and multivariate relationships between a high number of independent variables to a single dependent variable. Given a sufficient sample size, and with appropriate training and testing splits, these models are robust and can be operated to avoid overfitting. This model was applied to all taxa agglomerated at the subgenus level, or at the species level after removing species with a prevalence < 30%. This was performed on the relative taxa abundance, and 80% of the data were used for training and 20% for testing, over ten separate stability runs to obtain stable estimates of the model accuracy and avoid spurious results from certain sample combinations. The hyperparameters were tested using the train function (method = 'ranger’, importance = 'impurity’) from the caret package version 6.0-94, where the control was set to fivefold repeated cross-validation with three repeats and random search using the trainControl function. The hyperparameter grid used was: ntrees = (500 and 2000), nodesizes = (20, 50 and 80), splitrule = (variance, extratrees and beta), and mtry started at 5 to the maximum number of taxa, with a step size of 4 for subgenera, and a step size of 8 for species. The model parameters with the best median AUC calculated across all repeats was used to evaluate the model on the test set, using the function ranger (importance = impurity) from the package ranger version 0.15.1. The median test AUC of the ten stability runs was used to evaluate the model performance.

Procrustes analysis. Procrustes is a statistical method that compares two ordinations or matrices from, e.g. environmental and microbial data, by scaling (stretching) and rotating them to minimise the sum of squared differences. The protest function thereafter performs permutation of the Procrustes analysis repeatedly to estimate the significance of the Procrustes statistic and returns a correlation-like statistic from the symmetric Procrustes sum of squares. This was used to test associations between the bacteriophage composition and the anellovirus composition (N = 647), and the association between the anellovirus composition and the 16S rRNA gene amplicon-sequencing-based bacterial composition (N = 611). The data were first re-normalised separately, e.g. the anelloviruses and bacteriophages were re-normalised to 100%. The ordination was created using the distance-based redundancy analysis (dbrda) function, conditioned on lane and sequencing depth, and the association between the two ordinations was assessed with the procrustes function (symmetric = TRUE) and tested with the protest function (9999 permutations), all from the vegan package version 2.6-4.

SpiecEasi analysis. SPIEC-EASI (SParse InversE Covariance Estimation for Ecological Association Inference) is a method for identifying ecological networks among microbes (Kurtz et al. 2015). The SpiecEasi package version 0.1.4 was applied to all taxa agglomerated at the subgenus level, with the following settings: method = ‘mb’, lambda.min.ratio = 1e-1, nlambda = 50.

P value threshold for significance. All p values were considered significant at the nominal p < 0.05 level, or at the multiple testing adjusted (p.adjust function with method fdr) p < 0.05 level as noted. All statistical tests were two-tailed.

No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. No data were excluded from the analyses.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This paper by Boulund, et al, describes fecal anellovirus populations in 1 year old infants from a very large study of 647 one year old children from the Copenhagen Prospective Studies on Asthma in Childhood study. This is an incredible resource in terms of samples and clinical data for analysis.

The general process used for analyzing the samples is as follows: Sequence data was generated from filtered stool samples in order to analyze viruses present in the stool. Sequences were assembled and analyzed as viral OTUs. Prevalence and relative abundance of anelloviruses were associated with various clinical correlates using a variety of statistical tests.
While these steps are generally reasonable, there is an absence of critical experimental details that are needed to interpret the results.

Line 282: “…previous studies have suggested potential links to chronic diseases and immune system development.”
Citation needed.

Citations are given for the extraction and sequencing are given, but more detail is needed to describe what exactly is done in this paper.
- What amount of stool was used for virome extraction?
- How was DNA extracted? Kit?
- Was anything done to determine how effective the viral enrichment was? What proportion of the sequence reads generated were viral? Eukaryotic viruses?
- What proportion of sequences were not included in assemblies/analysis of vOTUs?
- Average depth, 3Gbp. Range? Was read depth used to scale results at any point?
- Should add into discussion biases that would be introduced by using MDA. You would be more likely to get small circular viruses like anelloviruses from MDA amplified samples than other DNA viruses that might be present. It seems surprising to only have anelloviruses and adenoviruses representing eukaryotic viruses in your data set. Is there other support for this observation or should it be explained by technical choices? Are other eukaryotic viruses detected in the individual sequencing reads but not assembled or identified in vOTUs?
- How were reads de-replicated?
- How were reads assembled?
- How were condigs deduplicated?
- If vOTUs are based on gene clusters, is there an overestimate of different viral species? For example, are vOTU from gene 1 and vOTU from gene 2 counted as two different taxa since we do not know if they are from the same genome or not? How are OTUs from different genes incorporated into the neighbor joining trees?
- Methods for tree needed
- How is relative abundance calculated? By contigs or underlying reads? Based on eukaryotic viruses? All viruses? Viruses and bacteria?
- How are diversity metrics calculated? Contigs #’s? All viruses? What taxonomic level?

Figures are not legible, so it is not possible to fully evaluate the results. Font is too small and blurry.

Some connections between points in results and discussion are a little unclear. For example:
Discussion: “By contrast, the anellovirus and the bacteriome compositions were not associated.”
Results: “There was a slight negative correlation between the gut microbial maturation score and the overall relative anelloviral abundance.”
Both things may be true, but a little clarification of exactly what is meant in each statement is needed.

The use of relative abundance sometimes makes interpretation difficult. For example, in the discussion: “The most consistent and strong effect on the anellovirus composition was whether the child had started day care before the sample collection.” Is there any way this could be explained by changes in abundance or diversity in bacteria or phage composition? It seems likely that it would have a big effect since daycare exposure is likely to increase diversity in the gut, as has been previously shown.

With some additional work and clarification, this work will be of interest to the field of human virome research.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Early life factors shaping infant gut anellovirus composition and associations with childhood atopic disease
General Comments
The strength of the study is the sample size and that this is part of a well-characterised cohort. I find that the most interesting output is that the Anelloviridae composition was associated with whether the child had started day care before the sample collection, which was also significantly associated with a reduced Anelloviruses alpha diversity and abundance. This is because there is a well characterised link between day care, infections, and the shift of the eukaryotic virome.

I find the inclusion of bacteriophages and Adenoviruses not efficiently justified in this study and I suggest that they are removed. The discussion around the relative abundance of Anelloviruses within the total virome is not supported scientifically since the data have not been appropriately normalised to allow for such analysis. For example, genome size can significantly affect relative abundances since fragments of larger genomes have higher probability of detection by shotgun sequencing. Also, the authors have not analysed the differential effect that sample processing, DNA extraction and MDA has in different virus groups. E.g. Differences in the GC, AT, and nucleotide sequence repeats of Anelloviruses and bacteriophages. I do not think the inclusion of 16S data is relevant either since a link between Anelloviruses and the bacteriome is not easily justified.

The authors have not adequately described the analytical pipelines and they often reference previous studies which I find problematic. My main scepticism is for the fact that the authors have not included negative controls and whole process negative controls in their strategy nor have they screened the reagents for Anelloviruses. In addition, they have not verified the presence of the Anelloviruses species using a second approach to provide confidence on the efficiency of their methods. There is an available Anelloviruses nester PCR available that could use in combination with sequencing to verify results at least in a fraction of samples. Or, have they been able to isolate any Anelloviruses species from the samples?

The metanalysis could also be significantly improved by unsupervised clustering of the samples based on Anelloviridae composition and then look for statistical association with outcomes. Dirichlet clustering could work nicely because it takes into account the lost biosphere effect of metagenomic datasets. Finally, different arbitrary thresholds are used throughout the metanalysis that confuses the reader and it is difficult to evaluate their meaning.

The authors need to be very careful when they discuss about Anelloviruses infection versus presence and clarify every time these terms are used.

Overall, I believe that the manuscript cannot be published as it is and will need major restructuring and additional experiments.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript titled “Early Life Factors Shaping Infant Gut Anellovirus Composition and Associations with Childhood Atopic Disease” by Boulund et al. focuses on factors that may influence the anelloviral community in the gastrointestinal tract of young children and explores potential links with atopic disease. The study identifies several associations between social, environmental, and genetic factors and the anellovirus community; however, none were found with atopic disease, except for a weak association with rhinitis and allergic sensitization. The key takeaway from a clinical perspective is that the child cohort under investigation is large enough to support the credibility of these negative findings.

Major Comment:
From the perspective of the readership of Nature Communications, it is questionable whether the presented data is comprehensive enough for publication in this forum. In its current form, the manuscript primarily reports microbial data without correlating it to clinical or immune functional data, which should be available in the cohort.

While this is a highly interesting and important field with many unresolved questions about the influence of anellovirus on physiology and immune competence, it would be of utmost interest to learn more about the potential role that anellovirus might play in the maturation of the microbiome, its possible association with host immune responses, and whether anellovirus could serve as a biomarker of immune function.

Minor Comments:
In lines 121 and 128, please clarify for non-bioinformatician readers what the functon("AND" >35%) means.
Do the anellovirus profiles in the children resemble those of their mothers?
Line 294: The results in the preceding lines were also not significant. Therefore, it is not accurate to state in this sentence that “no other results were significant.”

Point-by-point response to reviewer comments
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This paper by Boulund, et al, describes fecal anellovirus populations in 1 year old infants from a
very large study of 647 one year old children from the Copenhagen Prospective Studies on
Asthma in Childhood study. This is an incredible resource in terms of samples and clinical data
for analysis.
The general process used for analyzing the samples is as follows: Sequence data was
generated from filtered stool samples in order to analyze viruses present in the stool.
Sequences were assembled and analyzed as viral OTUs. Prevalence and relative abundance of
anelloviruses were associated with various clinical correlates using a variety of statistical tests.
While these steps are generally reasonable, there is an absence of critical experimental details that
are needed to interpret the results.
Answer: We appreciate the comments from the reviewer and have updated the manuscript to
include more details regarding the experimental design and process.
1. Line 282: “…previous studies have suggested potential links to chronic diseases
and immune system development.” Citation needed.
Regarding chronic diseases, we referenced in the introduction for example IBD (DOI:
10.1016/j.cell.2015.01.002) and asthma (DOI: 10.3389/fmicb.2018.00686, 10.1186/s12866-024-
03187-7 and 10.3390/v14020278), which we have now added to this particular sentence.
Furthermore, there are hypotheses regarding anellovirus influence on immune system
modulation and development in early life (DOI: 10.2174/0929867324666171005112921,
10.1093/femsre/fuaa007), we have now added these citations to the manuscript as well, please
see lines 256-257.
Citations are given for the extraction and sequencing are given, but more detail is needed to
describe what exactly is done in this paper.
Answer: We agree that the original version of this manuscript was too sparse in regards to the
details of the methods, and as such we have added extensively to this section. Please see the
specific answers below.
2. - What amount of stool was used for virome extraction?
This has now been detailed in the methods, please see lines 500-501. The original stool
samples were collected via small spoons from the collection tube, and 2 spoonfuls were
preserved in a 10% glycerol and beef broth stock solution (1mL), before freezing in -80C. For
the virome extractions, 300 ul of this stock was thawed per sample, corresponding to
approximately 150 mg faecal material.
3. - How was DNA extracted? Kit?
This was mentioned in the Methods section “Faecal sample collection, virome extraction and
computational processing” on lines 511-514; The virome libraries were prepared following the
manufacturer’s directions for the Illumina Nextera XT kit (FC-131-1096) and sequenced on the
Illumina HiSeq X platform (2 x 150 bp paired-end reads).
4. - Was anything done to determine how effective the viral enrichment was? What
proportion of the sequence reads generated were viral? Eukaryotic viruses?
We have now added a reference to our previous description of this dataset
(https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-023-01345-7), and a summary of this in the methods section of
this paper, please see lines 508-511. In total, 51% of the reads mapped to non-viral sequence
clusters, while 49% of the reads mapped to vOTUs. It is estimated that approximately 1-2% of
the DNA in a faecal sample is of viral origin. With this in mind, the enrichment factor was
estimated to be between 25 and 50 times enrichment of viral DNA over cellular DNA when
compared to shotgun metagenomes for the same samples.
5. - What proportion of sequences were not included in assemblies/analysis of
vOTUs?
This has been clarified in the methods section, please see lines 516-519. While MDA
amplification allows for the detection and quantification of ssDNA viruses, it does introduce
redundancy in the sequenced reads such that multiple reads with the same sequence occur. In
addition, virome extractions often have short inserts, leading to sequencing adapters. For these
reasons, on top of the standard read quality thresholds (minimum PHRED quality and length),
we removed reads that were shorter than 32 bp after adapter removal, and we collapsed reads
that were identical in sequence. On average this filtering removed 78% (+/- 13%) of the raw
reads per sample. The filtered subset of reads, comprising on average 22% of the original
number of sequenced reads, was used for both assembly and mapping.
6. - Average depth, 3Gbp. Range? Was read depth used to scale results at any
point?
The range of sequencing depth per sample was 0.01 to 24.63Gbp (mean 3Gbps +/- 1.6 Gbps).
We have now added this to the methods, please see lines 511-514. The total number of reads
per sample was included as a technical covariate in statistical analyses when possible as
described in the particular methods sections, and was also noted in the methods section
“Technical covariates”, please see lines 617-621.
7. - Should add into discussion biases that would be introduced by using MDA. You
would be more likely to get small circular viruses like anelloviruses from MDA
amplified samples than other DNA viruses that might be present. It seems
surprising to only have anelloviruses and adenoviruses representing eukaryotic
2
viruses in your data set. Is there other support for this observation or should it be
explained by technical choices? Are other eukaryotic viruses detected in the
individual sequencing reads but not assembled or identified in vOTUs?
We have added some discussion of this and the potential limitations in the manuscript, please
see lines 426-431.
As the reviewer correctly notes, MDA amplification does introduce biases, with circular ssDNA
being preferentially amplified. We curated the assemblies manually and did not detect other
eukaryotic viruses in our data besides dsDNA adenoviruses and ssDNA anelloviruses. Most
human gut viruses are RNA viruses that would not have been amplified by our protocol.
There are some eukaryotic DNA viruses that have been identified in infant faeces previously,
that we did not identify in our data, e.g. Circoviridae, Geminiviridae, Nanoviridae, Parvoviridae,
Polyomaviridae, and Genomoviridae (DOI: 10.1038/nm.3950, 10.1073/pnas.1514285112,
10.1128/JCM.01589-12, 10.1371/journal.pone.0240958, 10.1016/j.chom.2023.01.003,
10.1186/s40168-019-0766-7, 10.1016/j.chom.2019.09.009). Nanoviridae have shorter genomes
and would be removed based on our contig length cutoff of 1000 bp. There may be biological
explanations for the variations in viral identification compared to our data, e.g. variations in
breastfeeding rate and duration, geographical area, and birth mode. Furthermore, in the majority
of the mentioned studies anelloviruses are by and large the most prevalent and abundant virus
identified. In several other studies (DOI: 10.1038/s41598-022-26707-9,
10.3389/fmicb.2018.01162) anelloviruses are sometimes the only DNA virus identified in infant
faeces. Similarly, it is generally believed that there is a very low abundance of eukaryotic
viruses in the gut of (adult) healthy individuals, besides anelloviridae (DOI: 10.1146/annurev-
micro-102215-095431). To conclude, the identification of adenoviruses and anelloviruses as the
only eukaryotic viruses in this dataset does not appear to be out of the ordinary in a biological
aspect.
However, as the reviewer astutely has noted, there could also be technical variations that can
explain this. Some of the previously mentioned studies utilised PCR rather than sequencing, or
mapped reads to viral databases. While those approaches are more sensitive to known viruses,
they ignore any viral dark matter, which still represents the majority of the viral diversity in
virome samples to date. Our method was based on assembly and conservative curation. Thus
we might have missed some minor groups of viruses, but any major groups were certainly
picked up, even if they showed no similarity to any known viruses in databases. We published
this manually curated infant gut virome data set in the baseline paper (DOI: 10.1038/s41564-
023-01345-7), and made all the identified viral sequences freely available as a database which
is now “frozen” to ensure reproducibility across any studies that wish to utilise this data set. This
study is based on that data set.
After the publication of our baseline paper, an automated virus-prediction bioinformatics tool,
geNomad, was published (DOI: 10.1038/s41587-023-01982-7) that performs on par with our
manual curation (previous tools lacked sensitivity). Motivated by the reviewer’s question, we ran
this pipeline on our data and found that it does pick up additional eukaryotic viruses, but only
3
detects 697 out of the 970 anelloviruses that we found manually. The additional eukaryotic
viruses that geNomad finds were 83 CRESS viruses (including 7 circoviruses) and 42
Genomoviridae. So some additional eukaryotic viral groups are present, albeit minor, and we
want to acknowledge that as a weakness of our approach. Virome annotation is still a new field
with ongoing development and new tools becoming available regularly. There is still no ground
truth or generally accepted method/pipeline that allows for an ideal balance between false
positives and false negatives, and there is currently ongoing research into how well these newly
developed pipelines perform on different types of data (DOI: 10.1186/s13059-024-03236-4).
Thus, for consistency, we aim to keep our high-quality dataset “locked” for the purpose of the
present study, where we would like to maintain that our curated database was the best available
option.
8. - How were reads de-replicated?
The trimmed reads were de-replicated with VSEARCH version 2.4.3. We have added this to the
methods, please see lines 515-518.
9. - How were reads assembled?
The reads were assembled using Spades version 3.10.1. We have added this to the methods,
please see lines 520-523.
10. - How were condigs deduplicated?
The contigs (1.5 million) were de-duplicated if they were above 1 kb in size, to 362,000 95% ANI
(average nucleotide identity) representatives. We have added this to the methods, please see
lines 520-523.
11. - If vOTUs are based on gene clusters, is there an overestimate of different viral
species? For example, are vOTU from gene 1 and vOTU from gene 2 counted as
two different taxa since we do not know if they are from the same genome or not?
How are OTUs from different genes incorporated into the neighbor joining trees?
After assembling contigs from each sample, contigs across samples were merged into vOTUs if
they showed more than 95% average nucleotide identity (ANI), i.e. at the DNA level. From these
vOTUs, which included bacteriophages etc., the group of vOTUs that corresponded to
Anelloviruses was identified by their clustering at the protein-level. Although anelloviruses are
extremely diverse in sequence, they all appear to encode the same proteins, albeit in highly
divergent forms. This protein-level similarity is what we used to isolate anelloviruses as a group,
not to infer taxonomy. The neighbour joining tree that we constructed to sort out anelloviral
taxonomy was based on whole-genome DNA alignments, so does not contain gene-information
explicitly. We hope this answers the reviewers question and are happy to elaborate here or in
the manuscript if needed.
12. - Methods for tree needed
The methods for the tree were described in the Methods section “Faecal sample collection,
virome extraction and computational processing”, please see lines 526-547.
4
13. - How is relative abundance calculated? By contigs or underlying reads?
Based on eukaryotic viruses? All viruses? Viruses and bacteria?
We have expanded this in the methods, please see lines 527-530. Reads from each sample
were mapped against the global vOTU set (described in question 11 above), and individual
vOTU abundances were estimated by normalising the total read count per vOTU against the
length of that vOTU, as well as the total number of quality controlled reads in the sample. Thus,
the abundances are estimated based on read mapping to the assembled vOTUs. This was done
for all viruses, including bacteriophages, but not bacteria. The total relative abundance per
sample is thus 100% for the entire virome. Hereafter, depending on the analyses, the dataset
was subset to e.g. adenoviruses or anelloviruses, without re-normalisation.
14. - How are diversity metrics calculated? Contigs #’s? All viruses? What
taxonomic level?
All diversity metrics were calculated solely based on anelloviruses (or e.g. adenoviruses or
bacteriophages in Figure 1C), however the relative abundance included all viruses, as
described above. The alpha diversity metrics were calculated on the species level, whereas the
beta diversity metrics were calculated on the vOTU level, please see methods section “Alpha
and beta diversity calculations”, lines 623-644.
15. Figures are not legible, so it is not possible to fully evaluate the results. Font is
too small and blurry.
Thank you for pointing this out, the figures lost quality when submitted directly in the word
document. We have now included all the figures as high-quality PDFs which are present at the
end of the submitted document. Each panel can be zoomed in individually with high resolution.
16. Some connections between points in results and discussion are a little unclear.
For example: Discussion: “By contrast, the anellovirus and the bacteriome
compositions were not associated.” Results: “There was a slight negative
correlation between the gut microbial maturation score and the overall relative
anelloviral abundance.” Both things may be true, but a little clarification of exactly
what is meant in each statement is needed.
We understand that this is not entirely clear and have now added further explanation of this to
the manuscript, please see lines 248-250 and 307-308. The gut microbial maturation score is a
score calculated and presented in a previous study from the same 1-year faecal samples (DOI:
10.1038/s41467-017-02573-2). This is a normalised score that is related to the overall
maturation of the gut bacterial microbiome in early life. We hypothesised that the microbial
maturation of the gut microbiome may be related to immune development and thus the overall
abundance of anellovirus, which we also believe is related to immune development. However,
this does not necessarily mean that the actual microbial composition is related to the anellovirus
composition.
17. The use of relative abundance sometimes makes interpretation difficult. For
example, in the discussion: “The most consistent and strong effect on the
anellovirus composition was whether the child had started day care before the
5
sample collection.” Is there any way this could be explained by changes in
abundance or diversity in bacteria or phage composition? It seems likely that it
would have a big effect since daycare exposure is likely to increase diversity in
the gut, as has been previously shown.
This is an excellent point raised. As we processed and sequenced the anelloviruses,
adenoviruses and bacteriophages together, it is impossible with the current data to fully
disentangle compositionally dependent effects. As you mentioned, the diversity and abundance
of bacteria and bacteriophages is known to increase in early life and some of this may be
influenced by the start of daycare (as suggested by some: e.g. DOI: 10.1038/s41522-021-
00265-w). However, we did not report significant findings between daycare and the microbial
beta diversity at the 1 year fecal samples in a previous study from the same cohort (Fig 3. DOI:
https://doi.org/10.1186/s41468-022-01305-z), similarly, we did not find a significant association
in the microbial alpha diversity (Faith’s PD and richness) and daycare (p > 0.05). This suggests
that there is no effect of daycare on the alpha or beta diversity of the bacteriome of our samples,
and by extension there should be little effect on the bacteriophageome as this reflects the
bacteriome.
Thus, our results regarding daycare, gestational age, older siblings, and microbiota maturity,
suggest that these are important factors in the overall anellovirus abundance and diversity, and
are likely not a remnant of a compositional effect of these factors on the bacteriophageome.
This is in line with findings and hypotheses from previous studies that demonstrate a
relationship between the immune system and anellovirome. However, as we state in the
discussion (lines 342-344), this must be validated in longitudinal studies that investigate the
anellovirome immediately before and after daycare initiation. These studies could make use of
e.g. PCR or other quantitative methods to avoid the complications of compositionality.
With some additional work and clarification, this work will be of interest to the field of human
virome research.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Early life factors shaping infant gut anellovirus composition and associations with childhood
atopic disease
General Comments
The strength of the study is the sample size and that this is part of a well-characterised cohort. I
find that the most interesting output is that the Anelloviridae composition was associated with
whether the child had started day care before the sample collection, which was also significantly
associated with a reduced Anelloviruses alpha diversity and abundance. This is because there
is a well characterised link between day care, infections, and the shift of the eukaryotic virome.
Answer: We greatly appreciate the reviewers notice of some of the strengths of this study, and
a shared interest in some of the strongest findings.
I find the inclusion of bacteriophages and Adenoviruses not efficiently justified in this study and I
suggest that they are removed. The discussion around the relative abundance of Anelloviruses
within the total virome is not supported scientifically since the data have not been appropriately
normalised to allow for such analysis. For example, genome size can significantly affect relative
abundances since fragments of larger genomes have higher probability of detection by
shotgun sequencing. Also, the authors have not analysed the differential effect that sample processing,
DNA extraction and MDA has in different virus groups. E.g. Differences in the GC,
AT, and nucleotide sequence repeats of Anelloviruses and bacteriophages. I do not think the
inclusion of 16S data is relevant either since a link between Anelloviruses and the
bacteriome is not easily justified.
Answer: We regret that the rationale for our analysis of the entire virome at the outset of this
study was not clear. We have clarified this throughout the specific questions raised by the
reviewer, as well as in the manuscript itself.
The authors have not adequately described the analytical pipelines and they often reference
previous studies which I find problematic. My main scepticism is for the fact that the authors
have not included negative controls and whole process negative controls in their strategy nor
have they screened the reagents for Anelloviruses. In addition, they have not verified the
presence of the Anelloviruses species using a second approach to provide confidence on the
efficiency of their methods. There is an available Anelloviruses nester PCR available that could
use in combination with sequencing to verify results at least in a fraction of samples. Or,
have they been able to isolate any Anelloviruses species from the samples?
Answer: We have now added a considerable amount of detail to describe the analytical
pipelines used in this manuscript. Additionally, we included information on the whole process
negative controls that were included in the analysis, including the fact that the negative controls
did not contain any anelloviruses. Unfortunately we have limited faecal material left over from
these 14 year old samples, and this prohibits us from performing PCR on the faecal samples.
However, we have conducted an in silico PCR based on the method suggested (DOI:
10.1128/JCM.01703-07). We identified 970 vOTUs to be anelloviruses based on sequencing
and assembly, out of these 970, 869 (90%) contained one or more exact (100%) matches to the
primers described in the article, while 275 (28%) vOTUs contained exact 100% matches to the
sense/antisense pairs of the universal primers. There were no children that did not have any of
the 275 in silico PCR-identified anelloviruses (mean 40, range 3-162 per child). The average
prevalence among samples of these 275 in silico PCR-identified anelloviruses was 84 (median
78, range 6-461), out of our 647 samples. It is not expected that all anelloviruses identified with
our sequencing and computational processing will match 100% with the primers, especially
7
considering the very high genetic diversity among anelloviruses. However, based on the
phylogenetic tree that we created with several known anellovirus species, all anelloviruses
identified in this study are placed to be more similar to each other compared to the outgroup:
iotatorquevirus, an anellovirus species that infects non-human mammals. With this, we believe
the DNA extraction, sequencing and subsequent computational processing that lead to the
identification of anelloviruses in our samples is reliable and robust.
The metanalysis could also be significantly improved by unsupervised clustering of the samples
based on Anelloviridae composition and then look for statistical association with outcomes.
Dirichlet clustering could work nicely because it takes into account the lost biosphere effect of
metagenomic datasets. Finally, different arbitrary thresholds are used throughout the
metanalysis that confuses the reader and it is difficult to evaluate their meaning.
The authors need to be very careful when they discuss about Anelloviruses infection versus
presence and clarify every time these terms are used.
Overall, I believe that the manuscript cannot be published as it is and will need major
restructuring and additional experiments.

into contigs for each sample separately. Then contigs from all samples were pooled and subject
to an all-against-all DNA sequence alignment. Sequences which exhibited an ANI over 95%
were clustered into vOTUs, corresponding to the species-level cutoff for bacteriophages. For
12
anellovirus, this would be strain-level. Protein-coding ORFs were identified on all vOTUs and
their encoded protein sequences were subject to another all-against-all protein alignment to

ANI). These cutoffs closely match the ICTVs own criteria at 54% AND for genera and 65% AND

100% - ANI). This has now been clarified in the methods.

29. L603: Define terminology for ecological indexes.
We have now included a description of the ecological indices presented in the manuscript,
please see lines 623-44.
Faith’s Phylogenetic Diversity (PD): Measures the total evolutionary branch lengths represented
by taxa in a community, reflecting their phylogenetic relationships.
Shannon’s Diversity Index: Combines taxa richness and evenness to measure the uncertainty in
predicting the taxa of a randomly selected individual, where higher values indicate greater
diversity.
Aitchison Distance: Measures distance based on log-ratio transformations.
Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity: Quantifies the dissimilarity based on taxa abundances, emphasising
the proportion of shared versus unique taxa.
Jaccard Distance: Measures the distance by comparing the number of shared species to the
total number of species, ignoring abundances.

We understand that it may seem extreme to only analyse species that were present in >50% of
the samples, however this filtering threshold proved a suitable balance between multiple testing
burden and statistical power, while still analysing the vast majority of the anellovirus composition
(80% of the average anellovirus abundance per sample). We have described this in more detail

rationale behind this choice, including two figures to illustrate this.
It is standard practice to filter out taxa in microbiome analysis, with the thresholds chosen being
data, methodology, and hypothesis dependent. We find it important to highlight that the low-
prevalent and low-abundant species were considered in the alpha and beta diversity analyses
(including the procrustes analysis), as no filtering was conducted there. Regarding the
differential abundance and indicator species analysis, we decided to filter out species to reduce
the number of variables to test, i.e. to reduce the multiple testing burden, as these two analyses
are statistically independent tests per individual taxa. Furthermore, the power of the statistical
test is reduced when many samples do not have a taxon present, further reinforcing the need to
remove species that are only present in few samples.
This is also important when considering the biological interpretability of the results, identifying a
potential significant differential abundance in a species that was only present in very few
samples or that had a very low relative abundance can be considered of low clinical relevance,
as it is not likely to be generalisable to other populations. However, there are of course many
considerations and trade-offs between statistical power, multiple testing burden, and potential
clinical relevance and interpretability of the findings. Removing species that were present in less
than 50% of the population resulted in a dataset of 38 species out of 111, and these species
corresponded to on average 81% of the relative anellovirus abundance per sample. We believe
this is an appropriate balance between reducing the feature search space to reduce multiple
testing burden and maintain statistical power, while still evaluating an accurate and
representative anellovirome composition in the samples. We created two figures that illustrate

We believe employing both differential abundance and indicator species analysis provide a

Clustering is a non-robust methodology that is completely dependent on the samples included,
i.e. including or excluding a single sample may have vast impacts on the results, which limits the
generalisability of such methods and findings to future research and clinical interpretation. There
are many choices to be made when performing clustering, which we do not have answers to
from the previous literature. Most clustering methods are dependent on a predefined number of
clusters, but to this end, there is no previous data that can be used to estimate the appropriate
number of clusters to investigate. We could potentially generate anywhere between 2-70
clusters, but we do not have any previous studies providing us with a direction in this choice.
We do not know how many anellovirus species we can expect to find in a single cluster based
on a biological relationship. Should the clustering be performed on species or subgenus
taxonomy level?
To summarise, clustering is a simplification of an ecology, and we believe that the analysis we
have presented in this manuscript that are conducted on alpha and beta diversity, as well as
18
species, subgenus, genus and family level of anelloviruses are more comprehensive and
informative to the field than clustering which is completely data and cohort dependent and would
be difficult to recapitulate or replicate in future studies.
33. L641, L663, and 683: Here you use different thresholds. There needs to be
consistency when using arbitrary assigned thresholds across the different tests.
As it is now it looks as fishing for a significant association. Describe the filtered
subsets? How your results change from non-filtered to 100% with increments of
10%? What will mean if you see differences?
First of all, a distinction must be made when discussing subsetting of features vs. subsetting of
samples. Subsetting of samples was done for cross-validation, which is a common and robust,
widely agreed upon practice for minimising spurious findings. The 80/20 ratio is the most widely
used across all fields that employ statistical modelling to ensure robustness and accuracy of the
findings to avoid spurious findings and thus cannot be considered arbitrary.
In the methods of L641 (sPLS) and L663 (random forest, RF), the filtering thresholds are
entirely consistent; all subgenera are included, and species are included if their prevalence is
>30%. For the methods of L683 (Procrustes), no filtering is applied as this is a different
methodology that is based on ordinations of the dataset, not on individual taxa abundances. The
approach to this method is similar to the other methods we applied on beta diversity analysis,
which are also based on the entire composition and are not suitable to apply to filtered data.
For the analysis on differential abundance and indicator species analysis (DA/IS), a filtering
threshold was applied to the species level keeping only species that were present in >50% of
the population. We described the motivation for this above in our response to question number
31, where you can also see two graphs describing the relationship between mean relative
abundance and prevalence, and the number of reads mapping to different prevalence subsets.
The motivation for applying a different filter to the sPLS and RF models is based on the fact that
these models are inherently different from DA/IS. As we mentioned, DA/IS are independent
statistical tests, univariate tests, where the multiple testing burden increases drastically the
more taxa included for testing. Furthermore, the statistical power for low-prevalent species is
also decreased. sPLS and RF on the other hand are multivariable models, they do not test each
anellovirus species separately, and thus the multiple testing burden is not applicable to these
tests. However, these methods are highly complex and may be prone to overfitting if too many
irrelevant features are included. Thus, we decided to apply a more lenient filtering threshold to
these models as a means to reduce model complexity and risk of overfitting, while still
maintaining interpretability and utilising the power of these models, i.e. the fact that we can
analyse many more species in one test. The 30% prevalence filtering applied to sPLS/RF
results in 64 anellovirus species being included, which corresponds to on average 93% of the
relative abundance per sample. This results in a multivariate analysis that encompasses a great
coverage of the anellovirome composition per sample, while still removing low-prevalent
features that may increase overfitting and thus reduce model interpretability and clinical
19
relevance of the findings. This threshold was decided a priori based on a technical
understanding of the methodologies and considering the biological and clinical interpretability of
the findings.
We believe that applying the same methodology across the full range of species prevalence
(from 0% to 100%) may not be the most appropriate approach, especially given the distinct
strengths and weaknesses of each model, as we outlined earlier. Including all species in the
analysis would likely lead to overfitting, producing spurious results with limited clinical relevance.
Therefore, any differences observed based on the prevalence filter are more likely to reflect
variations in model overfitting or underfitting, rather than biologically or clinically meaningful
findings. As we demonstrated in the answer to your question 31, analyses on species present in
<30% of samples would likely lead to spurious results as they cover a very small proportion of
the abundance.
To further support this point, we have reanalyzed the sPLS model at the species level for atopic
dermatitis at 6 years of age, using different filtering thresholds. This is summarised in the table
below, demonstrating that the filtering threshold applied has minimal impact on the findings
presented in this manuscript, and does not alter the conclusions of our study at all. This is likely
due to the fact that the vast majority of the anellovirus abundance remains well-represented,
even with relatively high prevalence filtering thresholds. Thus, the anelloviruses with lower
prevalence exhibit such minimal abundance that their contribution to the model’s predictions is
negligible.
